¶
{{smaller block|I myself have seen one of these male ''Abigails'' tripping about the room with a looking-glass in his hand and combing his lady’s hair a whole morning together.
{{right|''Spectator.''}}}}

'''abigeat''' (ab-ij′ẹ̄-at), ''n.'' [< OF. ''abigeat'', < L. ''abigeatus'', cattle-stealing, < ''abigeus'', a cattle-stealer, < ''abigere'', drive away: see ''abactor.'' For the second sense (''b''), cf. L. ''abiga'', a plant which has the power of producing abortion, < ''abigere'', as above.] In ''law'': (''a'') The crime of stealing or driving off cattle in droves. (''b'') A miscarriage procured by art.

'''abiliate†''' (ạ-bil′i-āt), ''v. t.'' [For ''abilitate''; or irreg. formed from ''able'', L. ''habilis'', ML. (''h'')''abilis''.] To enable. ''Bacon.'' [Rare.]

'''abiliment†''' (ạ-bil′i-mẹnt), ''n.'' [Var. of ''habiliment'', q. v.] Ability: as, “''abiliment'' to steer a kingdom,” ''Ford'', Broken Heart, v. 2.

'''abiliments†''', ''n. pl.'' Same as ''habiliments''.

'''abilitate†''' (ạ-bil′i-tāt), ''v. t.'' [<ML. ''habilitatus'', pp. of ''habilitare'' (> OF. ''habileter'', ''habiliter''), render able, < ''habilis'', able: see ''able''<sup>1</sup>.] To assist. ''Nicholas Ferrar.''

'''ability''' (ạ-bil′i-ti), ''n.'' [< ME. ''abilite'' (four syllables), < OF. ''habilite'' (ME. also ''ablete'', < OF. ''ablete''), < L. ''habilita''(''t-'')''s'', ML. ''abilita''(''t-'')''s'', aptness, < ''habilis'', apt, able: see ''able''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' The state or condition of being able; power or capacity to do or act in any relation; competence in any occupation or field of action, from the possession of capacity, skill, means, or other qualification.
{{smaller block|They gave after their ''ability'' unto the treasure of the work.
{{right|Ezra ii. 69.}}}}

<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="proofreader" />{{RunningHeader|abhor|11|ability}}</noinclude>{{nop}}'''II.''' ''intrans.'' '''1†.''' To shrink back with disgust, or with fear and shudderings.
{{smaller block|To ''abhorre'' from those vices.
{{right|''Udall'', Erasmus, St. James, iv.}}}}
'''2.''' To be antagonistic; be averse or of opposite character: with ''from.''
{{smaller block|Which is utterly ''abhorring from'' the end of all law.
{{right|''Milton'', Divorce, II. vii. 79.}}}}

'''abhorrence''' (ab-hor′e̤ns), ''n.''  [< ''abhorrent'': see ''-ance.'']  '''1.''' The act of abhorring; a feeling of extreme aversion or detestation; strong hatred.
{{smaller block|One man thinks justice consists in paying debts, and has no measure in his ''abhorrence'' of another who is very remiss in this duty.
{{right|''Emerson'', Essays, 1st ser., p. 286.}}}}
'''2†.''' An expression of abhorrence. {{smaller|Specifically, an address presented in 1680 to Charles II. of England, expressing abhorrence of the Addressers (which see).}}

'''3.''' That which excites repugnance or loathing: as, servility is my ''abhorrence.'' = {{smaller|'''Syn. 1.''' Horror, hatred, detestation, repugnance, disgust, loathing, shrinking, antipathy, aversion.}}

'''abhorrency†''' (ab-hor′e̤n-si), ''n.'' The quality of being abhorrent, or the state of regarding anything with horror or loathing.
{{smaller block|The first tendency to any injustice . . . must be suppressed with a show of wonder and ''abhorrency'' in the parents.
{{right|''Locke'', Education, ¶ 110.}}}}

'''abhorrent''' (ab-hor′e̤nt), ''a.''  [< L. ''abhorren(t-)s'', ppr. of ''abhorrere'': see ''abhor.'']  '''1.''' Hating; detesting; struck with abhorrence.
{{smaller block|<poem>The arts of pleasure in despotic courts
I spurn ''abhorrent.''</poem>
{{right|''Glover'', Leonidas, x.}}}}
'''2.''' Exciting horror or abhorrence; very repulsive; detestable: as, ''abhorrent'' scenes; an ''abhorrent'' criminal or course of conduct.—'''3.''' Contrary; utterly repugnant; causing aversion: formerly with ''from'', now with ''to''.
{{smaller block|And yet it is so ''abhorrent from'' the vulgar.
{{right|''Glanville'', Scep. Sci.}}}}
{{smaller block|Christianity turns from these scenes of strife, as ''abhorrent to'' her highest injunctions. {{right|''Sumner'', Aug. 27, 1846.}}}}

'''abhorrently''' (ab-hor′ẹnt-li), ''adv.'' With abhorrence; in an abhorrent manner.

'''abhorrer''' (ab-hôr′ėr), ''n.'' One who abhors. {{smaller|Specifically (with or without a capital letter), in the reign of Charles II. of England, a member of the court party, afterward called Tories. They derived their name from their professed abhorrence of the principles of the Addressers, who endeavored to restrict the royal prerogative. See ''addresser''.}}
{{smaller block|Scarce a day passed but some ''abhorrer'' was dragged before them [the House of Commons] and committed to the custody of the sergeant-at-arms, at the pleasure of the house. {{right|''Roger North'', Examen, p. 561.}}}}

'''abhorrible''' (ab-hor′i-bl), ''a.''  [< ''abhor'' + ''-ible'', after ''horrible''.]  Worthy or deserving to be abhorred. [Rare.]

'''abhorring''' (ab-hôr′ing), ''n.'' '''1.''' A feeling of abhorrence; loathing.
{{smaller block|I find no ''abhorring'' in my appetite. {{right|''Donne'', Devotion.}}}}
'''2†.''' An object of abhorrence.
{{smaller block|They shall be an ''abhorring'' unto all flesh. {{right|Isa. lxvi. 24.}}}}

'''abhul''', ''n.'' See ''abhal''.

'''Abia''' (ā′bi-ä̤), ''n.'' A genus of ''Hymenoptera''.  ''Leach.''

'''Abib''' (ā′bib), ''n.''  [Heb. ''ābīb'', an ear of corn, < ''ābab'', produce early fruit, < ''āb'', swelling.]  The time of newly ripe grain; the first month of the Jewish ecclesiastical year, beginning with the new moon of March. {{smaller|''Abib'' seems to have been the designation of a season rather than the name of a month. After the Babylonish captivity it was also called ''Nisan'' (Neh. ii. 1).}}

'''abidance''' (a̤-bī′dans), ''n.''  [< ''abide''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ance.'']  The act of abiding or continuing; abode; stay.  ''Fuller.'' [Rare.]
{{smaller block|And then, moreover, there is His personal ''abidance'' in our churches, raising earthly service into a foretaste of heaven.
{{right|''J. H. Newman'', Gram. of Assent, p. 475.}}}}

'''abide'''<sup>1</sup> (a̤-bīd′), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''abode'', ppr. ''abiding.''  [< ME. ''abiden'' (pret. sing. ''abod'', pl. ''abiden'', pp. ''abiden''), < AS. ''ābīdan'' (pret. sing. ''ābād'', pl. ''ābidon'', pp. ''ābiden'') (= Goth. ''usbeidan'', expect), < ''ā-'' + ''bīdan'', bide: see ''bide.'' The ME. and AS. forms are trans. and intrans.]  '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To wait for; especially, to stand one’s ground against.
{{smaller block|''Abide'' me if thou dar’st.
{{right|''Shak.'', M. N. D., iii. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|Howbeit we ''abide'' our day!
{{right|''M. Arnold'', Balder Dead.}}}}
'''2.''' To await; be in store for.
{{smaller block|Bonds and afflictions ''abide'' me.
{{right|Acts xx. 23.}}}}
'''3.''' To endure or sustain; remain firm under.
{{smaller block|Who may ''abide'' the day of his coming?
{{right|Mal. iii. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|Greatness does not need plenty, and can very well ''abide'' its loss.
{{right|''Emerson'', Essays, 1st ser., p. 232.}}}}
'''4.''' To put up with; tolerate. [In this colloquial sense approaching ''abide''<sup>2</sup>.]
{{smaller block|I cannot ''abide'' the smell of hot meat.
{{right|''Shak.'', M. W. of W., i. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|As for disappointing them, I shouldn’t so much mind, but I can’t ''abide'' to disappoint myself.
{{right|''Goldsmith'', She Stoops to Conquer, i. 1.}}}}
'''5†.''' To encounter; undergo: in a jocular sense. [?]
{{smaller block|<poem>I wil give hym the alder-beste
Gifte, that ever he ''abode'' hys lyve.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Dethe of Blaunche, l. 247.}}}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To have one’s abode; dwell; reside.
{{smaller block|<poem>In the noiseless air and light that flowed
Round your fair brows, eternal Peace ''abode''.</poem>
{{right|''Bryant'', To the Apennines.}}}}
'''2.''' To remain; continue to stay.
{{smaller block|Except these ''abide'' in the ship, ye cannot be saved.
{{right|Acts xxvii. 31.}}}}
{{smaller block|Here no man can ''abide'', except he be ready with all his heart to humble himself for the love of God.
{{right|''Thomas à Kempis'', Im. of Christ, i. 17.}}}}
'''3.''' To continue in a certain condition; remain steadfast or faithful.
{{smaller block|But she is happier if she so ''abide'' [in widowhood].
{{right|1 Cor. vii. 40.}}}}
'''4†.''' To wait; stop; delay.
{{smaller block|<poem>He hasteth wel that wysly kan ''abyde''.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, i. 949.}}}}
'''5.''' To inhere; belong as an attribute or quality; have its seat.
{{smaller block|<poem>Though far more cause, yet much less spirit to curse
''Abides'' in me.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. III., iv. 4.}}}}

{{smaller|'''To abide by.''' (''a'') To remain at rest beside: as, “''abide by'' thy crib,” Job xxxix. 9. (''b'') To adhere to; maintain; defend; stand to: as, to ''abide by'' a friend. Specifically, in ''Scots law'', to adhere to as true and genuine: said of the party who relies upon a deed or writing which the other party desires to have reduced or declared null and void, on the ground of forgery or falsehood. (''c'') To await or accept the consequences of; rest satisfied with: as, ''abide by'' the event or issue. = '''Syn.''' '''1''' and '''2'''. ''Abide, Sojourn, Continue, Dwell, Reside, Live'', remain, stay, stop, lodge, settle, settle down, tarry, linger. ''Live'' is the most general word: to pass one’s life, without indicating place, time, or manner.  ''Abide, sojourn'', to stay for a time—length of stay being associated in the mind with the former, and briefness or shortness of stay with the latter. ''Continue'', to stay on, without interval of absence. ''Dwell'', to be domiciled. ''Reside'', to have one’s home; dwell.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>And if these pleasures may thee move,
Then ''live'' with me and be my love.</poem>
{{right|''Marlowe'', Shepherd to his Love.}}}}
{{smaller block|O Thou who changest not, ''abide'' with me!
{{right|''Lyte''.}}}}
{{smaller block|A certain man of Beth-lehem-judah went to ''sojourn'' in the country of Moab, he, and his wife, and his two sons. . . . And they came into the country of Moab, and ''continued'' there.
{{right|Ruth i. 1, 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|And Moses was content to ''dwell'' with the man.
{{right|Exod. ii. 21.}}}}
{{smaller block|There, at the moated grange, ''resides'' this dejected Mariana.
{{right|''Shak.'', M. for M., iii. 1.}}}}

'''abide'''<sup>2</sup> (ạ-bīd′), ''v. t.''  [This word in the sense of 'suffer for' does not occur much earlier than Shakspere’s time. It is a corruption of ME. ''abyen'', pay for, due to confusion with ''abide''<sup>1</sup>, wait for (as if that sense were equivalent to 'endure'): see further under ''aby''<sup>1</sup>, and cf. ''abide''<sup>1</sup>, ''v. t.'', 4.]  To pay the price or penalty of; suffer for.
{{smaller block|If it be found so, some will dear ''abide'' it.
{{right|''Shak.'', J. C., iii. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Ah me! they little know
How dearly I ''abide'' that boast so vain.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., iv. 86.}}}}

'''abident†'''. Old perfect participle of ''abide''<sup>1</sup>.

'''abider''' (ạ-bī′dėr), ''n.''  [< ''abide''<sup>1</sup> + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.]  One who dwells or continues; one who lives or resides.

'''abiding''' (a̤-bī′ding), ''p. a.''  [Ppr. of ''abide''<sup>1</sup>.]  Continuing; permanent; steadfast: as, an ''abiding'' faith.
{{smaller block|Here thou hast no ''abiding'' city.
{{right|''Thomas à Kempis'', Im. of Christ, ii. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|I do not think that Pope’s verse anywhere sings, but it should seem that the ''abiding'' presence of fancy in his best work forbids his exclusion from the rank of poet.
{{right|''Lowell'', Study Windows, p. 432.}}}}

'''abidingly''' (a̤-bī′ding-li), ''adv.'' In an abiding manner; enduringly; lastingly; permanently.

'''abiding-place''' (a̤-bī′ding-plās), ''n.''  [< ''abiding'', verbal n. of ''abide''<sup>1</sup>, + ''place''.]  A place where one abides; a permanent dwelling-place; hence, a place of rest; a resting-place.
{{smaller block|A very charming little ''abiding-place''.
{{right|''H. James, Jr.'', Trans. Sketches, p. 41.}}}}
{{smaller block|Many of these plants . . . found suitable ''abiding-places'' at the South. {{right|''Science'', III. 359.}}}}

'''Abies''' (ab′i-ēz), ''n.''  [L. ''abies'' (''abiet-''), the silver fir; origin unknown.]  A genus of trees, the firs, of the suborder ''Abietineæ'', natural order ''Coniferæ'', some of which are valuable for their timber. {{smaller|It differs from ''Pinus'' in its solitary leaves and in the thin scales of its cones, which ripen the first year. From the allied genera ''Picea'', ''Tsuga'', etc., with which it has sometimes been united, it is distinguished by its closely sessile leaves, by the bracts of the female aments being much larger than the scales, and by having erect cones with deciduous scales. It includes 16 or 18 species, confined to the northern hemisphere, and equally divided between the old and new worlds. To it belong the silver fir of central Europe (''A. pectinata''), the balsam-fir of eastern North America (''A. balsamea''), the red and white firs of western America (''A. grandis'', ''concolor'', and ''nobilis''), the sacred fir of Mexico (''A. religiosa''), etc. See ''fir''.}}

'''abietene''' (ab′i-ē-tēn), ''n.''  [< L. ''abies'' (''abiet-''), the fir, + ''-ene''.]  A hydrocarbon obtained by distillation from the resin of the nut-pine of California, ''Pinus Sabiniana''. {{smaller|It consists almost wholly of normal heptane, C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>16</sub>, and is a nearly colorless mobile liquid, having a strong aromatic smell, highly inflammable, and burning with a white, smokeless flame.}}

'''abietic''' (ab-i-et′ik), ''a.''  [< L. ''abies'' (''abiet-''), the fir, + ''-ic''.]  Of or pertaining to trees of the genus ''Abies''; derived from the fir.—{{smaller|'''Abietic acid''', C<sub>20</sub>H<sub>30</sub>O<sub>2</sub>, an acid obtained from the resin of some species of pine, larch, and fir. These resins are anhydrids of abietic acid or mixtures containing it.}}

'''abietin''' (ab′i-ē-tin), ''n.''  [< L. ''abies'' (''abiet-''), the fir, + ''-in''<sup>2</sup>.]  A tasteless, inodorous resin, derived from the turpentine obtained from some species of the genus ''Abies''.

'''Abietineæ''' (ab″i-ẹ̄-tin′ẹ̄-ē), ''n. pl.''  [NL., < L. ''abies'' (''abiet-''), the fir, + ''-in-eæ''.]  A suborder of the natural order ''Coniferæ'', distinguished by bearing strobiles (cones) with two inverted ovules at the base of each scale, which become winged samaroid seeds. {{smaller|The leaves are linear or needle-shaped, and never tworanked. It includes many of the most valuable kinds of timber-trees, viz., pine (''Pinus''), true cedar (''Cedrus''), spruce (''Picea''), hemlock-spruce (''Tsuga''), Douglas’s spruce (''Pseudotsuga''), fir (''Abies''), and larch (''Larix'').}} {{img float|file=century v01 p0037 c3f1.png|width=155px|align=right|cap={{smaller|(1) Staminate and (2) pistillate inflorescence of the pine; (3) a pistillate scale, and (4) the same showing a longitudinal section of the ovules.}}}}

'''abietinic''' (ab″i-ẹ̄-tin′ik), ''a.'' Pertaining to or derived from abietin: as, ''abietinic'' acid.

'''abietite''' (ab′i-ẹ̄-tīt), ''n.''  [< L. ''abies'' (''abiet-''), the fir, + ''-ite''<sup>2</sup>.]  A sugar, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O<sub>3</sub>, obtained from the needles of the European silver fir, ''Abies pectinata.''

'''Abietites''' (ab″i-ẹ̄-tī′tēz), ''n.''  [NL., pl. (sc. ''plantæ''), < L. ''abies'' (''abiet-''), the fir.]  A genus of fossil plants, natural order ''Coniferæ'', occurring in the Wealden and Lower Greensand strata.

'''Abigail''' (ab′i-gạ̄l), ''n.''  [< ''Abigail'', the “waiting gentlewoman” in Beaumont and Fletcher’s play of “The Scornful Lady”—so named, perhaps, in allusion to the expression “thine handmaid,” applied to herself by Abigail, the wife of Nabal, when carrying provisions to David: see 1 Sam. xxv. 2–41.]  A general name for a waiting-woman or lady’s-maid. [Colloq.] Sometimes written as a common noun, without a capital.
{{smaller block|The ''Abigail'', by immemorial custom, being a deodand, and belonging to holy Church.
{{right|''Reply to Ladies and Bachelors Petition'', 1694}}
{{right|(Harl. Misc., IV. 440).}}}}

{{smaller block|I myself have seen one of these male ''Abigails'' tripping about the room with a looking-glass in his hand and combing his lady’s hair a whole morning together.
{{right|''Spectator.''}}}}

'''abigeat''' (ab-ij′ẹ̄-at), ''n.''  [< OF. ''abigeat'', < L. ''abigeatus'', cattle-stealing, < ''abigeus'', a cattle-stealer, < ''abigere'', drive away: see ''abactor.'' For the second sense (''b''), cf. L. ''abiga'', a plant which has the power of producing abortion, < ''abigere'', as above.]  In ''law'': (''a'') The crime of stealing or driving off cattle in droves. (''b'') A miscarriage procured by art.

'''abiliate†''' (ạ-bil′i-āt), ''v. t.''  [For ''abilitate''; or irreg. formed from ''able'', L. ''habilis'', ML. (''h'')''abilis''.]  To enable.  ''Bacon.'' [Rare.]

'''abiliment†''' (ạ-bil′i-mẹnt), ''n.''  [Var. of ''habiliment'', q. v.]  Ability: as, “''abiliment'' to steer a kingdom,” ''Ford'', Broken Heart, v. 2.

'''abiliments†''', ''n. pl.'' Same as ''habiliments''.

'''abilitate†''' (ạ-bil′i-tāt), ''v. t.''  [<ML. ''habilitatus'', pp. of ''habilitare'' (> OF. ''habileter'', ''habiliter''), render able, < ''habilis'', able: see ''able''<sup>1</sup>.]  To assist.  ''Nicholas Ferrar.''

'''ability''' (ạ-bil′i-ti), ''n.''  [< ME. ''abilite'' (four syllables), < OF. ''habilite'' (ME. also ''ablete'', < OF. ''ablete''), < L. ''habilita''(''t-'')''s'', ML. ''abilita''(''t-'')''s'', aptness, < ''habilis'', apt, able: see ''able''<sup>1</sup>.]  '''1.''' The state or condition of being able; power or capacity to do or act in any relation; competence in any occupation or field of action, from the possession of capacity, skill, means, or other qualification.
{{smaller block|They gave after their ''ability'' unto the treasure of the work.
{{right|Ezra ii. 69.}}}}

{{smaller block|<poem>{{gap}}{{gap}}Alas! what poor
''Ability'''s in me to do him good?</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', M. for M., i. 5.}}}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
